flashcards.q: Explain the read-then-write race condition in MongoDB and why findOneAndUpdate fixes it.
flashcards.a: find() followed by a separate update() has an unprotected window where a concurrent request can read the same stale state and act on it too. findOneAndUpdate evaluates the filter condition and applies the mutation as ONE atomic server-side operation, eliminating the separate check step entirely.

flashcards.q: What is the trap that catches people who 'know' findOneAndUpdate exists?
flashcards.a: Performing a separate prior find() to DECIDE whether to call findOneAndUpdate, then building business logic on that separate read - this reintroduces the same race. The condition must be inside the atomic operation's filter, never evaluated in application code beforehand.

flashcards.q: Rank the five approaches to fixing a check-then-write race, cheapest to most expensive.
flashcards.a: 1) Atomic update operator with embedded condition (updateOne with filter condition). 2) findOneAndUpdate with conditional filter (need document back). 3) Optimistic concurrency via version field. 4) Unique/partial index (invariant is uniqueness). 5) Multi-document transaction (genuine cross-document invariant only).

flashcards.q: How does WiredTiger's document-level concurrency differ from MMAPv1?
flashcards.a: WiredTiger uses MVCC plus intent locking down to document level - only writers to the SAME document serialize, different documents proceed with zero contention. MMAPv1 locked at the collection level, blocking unrelated concurrent writes to the same collection.

flashcards.q: What is the unbounded array anti-pattern and why does it hurt before hitting the 16MB limit?
flashcards.a: An array that grows indefinitely inside a document eventually forces the document to exceed its allocated disk space, causing WiredTiger to relocate the WHOLE document on append - progressively worsening write latency well before the 16MB hard limit is reached.

flashcards.q: What is the fix for the unbounded array anti-pattern?
flashcards.a: The bucket pattern - group array elements into bounded sub-documents (e.g. one document per user per day, internally capped) - or move the growing data into its own referenced collection entirely.

flashcards.q: w:1 vs w:majority write concern - what's the durability difference during a primary failover?
flashcards.a: w:1 is acknowledged by the primary alone and can be ROLLED BACK if the primary fails before replicating it and a different secondary (without that write) becomes primary. w:majority requires majority acknowledgment, guaranteeing it survives any subsequent election.

flashcards.q: Read concern local vs majority vs linearizable?
flashcards.a: local: may be rolled back later (not majority-replicated yet). majority: only durable, non-rollback-able data. linearizable: strongest guarantee, confirms with a majority on EVERY read (real latency cost).

flashcards.q: What does a causally consistent session guarantee that plain readConcern:majority doesn't?
flashcards.a: Read-your-own-writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes, writes-follow-reads within a session - because different reads across the session could otherwise hit secondaries with different replication lag and appear to go backward in time.

flashcards.q: Why does a monotonically increasing shard key create a hot shard, and what's the fix?
flashcards.a: All new writes have the highest key value, landing on the single shard owning the top range - gets worse as write volume grows. Fix: hashed sharding spreads monotonic values pseudo-randomly across shards, at the cost of losing efficient range scans on that key.

flashcards.q: Three shard key selection criteria to check before committing to one?
flashcards.a: Cardinality (enough distinct values to split into chunks), monotonicity (increasing keys concentrate writes on one shard), skew (one dominant value creates a hot shard regardless of overall cardinality).

flashcards.q: Why is $lookup typically more expensive than a relational join?
flashcards.a: Fast only when the foreign collection has an index on the compared field (~nested loop with index); degrades to a full collection scan per input document without one - a much worse cost curve. Constant $lookup on a hot path signals the data should be embedded instead.

flashcards.q: When should you use multi-document transactions in MongoDB, and what's the schema smell if overused?
flashcards.a: Use for operations genuinely spanning multiple documents no embedding could avoid (e.g. funds transfer between two accounts). If most hot-path writes need transactions, that signals the schema should be redesigned around better embedding, not that transactions are simply 'the MongoDB way.'

flashcards.q: What do retryable writes solve, and how is that different from the application-level race condition problem?
flashcards.a: Retryable writes (default since 4.2) auto-retry on transient network/election failure using an idempotency token, solving 'did my write land exactly once.' This is orthogonal to the read-then-write race, which occurs even with perfect networking, purely from concurrent stale reads.

Wraps sharding and an immediate resharding-to-the-same-key into one operation, avoiding the historical pain of waiting on the background balancer to slowly redistribute data after an initial shard operation.
